opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's one of the things that gets me most excited right now. When most people think about latency in AI, they picture a single interaction: you type a prompt into a chatbot, you wait a second or two, and you get an answer. In that world, latency matters, but humans are fairly forgiving. If the response takes a little longer, you just sit there and read it as it streams out.

Agentic systems change that equation completely. With tools like OpenClaw, you're not making one call to a model. An agent might plan a task, break it into steps, call a tool, read the result, reason about it, call another model, check its own work, and loop. A single user request can fan out into dozens or even hundreds of inference calls chained together. Latency compounds across that chain. If each step adds a few hundred milliseconds, or a couple of seconds, suddenly the whole task takes minutes. At that point it doesn't feel like an assistant anymore; it feels like you submitted a batch job.

So latency goes from being a nice-to-have, user-experience metric to being a core determinant of what agents can actually do. Faster inference means an agent can take more reasoning steps within the same time budget, explore more options, verify more, and ultimately produce better results. Speed effectively becomes intelligence in an agentic world.

There's also the machine-to-machine aspect. Increasingly, agents talk to other agents, not people. There's no human patience to absorb the delay, and the systems are waiting on each other. Any slowness in one link stalls the whole pipeline.

And this is exactly why we've been so focused on inference at d-Matrix. For years the industry optimized hardware around training, where throughput is king and you can just throw massive batches at the problem. Inference, especially interactive, agentic inference, is a different beast. It's often memory-bound, it's latency-sensitive, and it's very cost-sensitive because it runs constantly, at scale. That pushes you toward architectures that keep data close to compute, minimize data movement, and deliver very fast token generation at low batch sizes, without blowing up the power budget.

So my view is that agentic AI is going to be the thing that really exposes the gap between hardware built for training and hardware built for inference. Latency is going to become one of the primary metrics people buy on, right alongside cost per token and energy efficiency. The companies that can deliver fast, efficient, interactive inference are going to unlock the agent economy everyone's talking about.

r001.rationale: The response says agents increasingly communicate with other agents, that systems wait on one another, and that slowness in one link stalls the whole pipeline.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Look, I think latency is going from being a nice-to-have to being the whole game, and agents are the reason.

For the last couple of years, the mental model for inference was a chatbot. A human types a question, the model thinks for a second or two, a response streams back, and the human reads it. Humans read at maybe 300 words a minute, so if you can generate tokens a bit faster than that, you're fine. Nobody noticed a few hundred milliseconds here or there. That model let a lot of people get comfortable with the idea that throughput is what matters and latency is secondary.

Agents break that completely. With something like OpenClaw, the model isn't talking to a person. It's talking to tools, to other models, to a file system, to a browser. It generates a plan, calls a tool, reads the result, reasons again, calls another tool. One user request might turn into fifty or a hundred model invocations chained together. And they're sequential. Step twelve can't start until step eleven finishes. So every bit of latency you have per call gets multiplied by the length of that chain. If each step takes two seconds, a hundred-step task takes three minutes. If each step takes two hundred milliseconds, it takes twenty seconds. That's the difference between an agent that feels like a coworker and one that feels like filing a ticket.

The other thing people underestimate is that nobody is reading those intermediate tokens. There's no human in the loop to hide the latency behind. So all the tricks we used in the chatbot era, streaming the first token quickly so the user sees something happening, those don't help at all. The agent needs the complete answer before it can act. What matters now is time to last token, not time to first token.

And this is where I think the hardware conversation gets interesting. GPUs were built for throughput. They're phenomenal at batching thousands of requests together and getting great aggregate tokens per second. But batching is fundamentally a latency tradeoff. You're waiting to fill the batch. For agentic workloads, where you have one chain of dependent calls that need to run as fast as possible, that architecture is working against you. You want hardware that can run a single sequence extremely fast, with memory bandwidth sitting right next to compute so you're not constantly shuttling weights around.

So my view is that agents are going to force a re-architecture of inference infrastructure. Latency becomes the primary design constraint, and the economics follow from that. The companies that figure out how to make these long reasoning chains fast are going to own the agentic era, because at some point users won't tolerate watching an agent think for five minutes to do something they could have done in three.

r001.rationale: The response says chained model calls are sequential, with each step waiting for the previous step, but it does not explain that agents must wait for other agents to finish tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think agentic tools make latency much more important. When you’re chatting with a model, you ask a question and wait for an answer. With an agent, that one request can trigger a whole sequence of steps: the model reasons, calls a tool, looks at the result, and decides what to do next. Those steps often depend on one another, so the delays add up.

If you want the agent to feel interactive—to actually work alongside you—you have to make that entire loop fast. It’s not just about how quickly the first token appears or how many tokens per second you generate. It’s about how long it takes to complete the task. As agents do more steps on your behalf, inference latency becomes a much bigger part of that experience.

r001.rationale: The response says an agent’s sequential reasoning and tool calls make delays add up, but it does not say agents must wait for other agents to finish tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think agentic tools make latency much more important because you’re no longer waiting for just one response. An agent might make a model call, use a tool, look at the result, and then decide what to do next. That can happen many times to complete a single task, and the delays compound.

So the question becomes: how quickly can the system finish useful work? Throughput still matters, but when each step depends on the previous one, you can’t solve everything by running more requests in parallel. You need fast responses throughout that loop. That’s what makes an agent feel like something you can work with interactively.

r001.rationale: The response says agent workflows have sequential, dependent model and tool steps whose delays compound. It does not explain that agents must wait for other agents to finish tasks.
